title: The Constitutional Convention
short: In 1787 delegates in Philadelphia replaced the Articles; the Great (Connecticut) Compromise blended the Virginia Plan (seats by population) and the New Jersey Plan (equal seats), and other compromises dealt with slavery and the presidency.
trouble: Students think the Three-Fifths Compromise said enslaved people were three-fifths of a person in law. It was a rule for counting population for House seats and direct taxes: three of every five enslaved people were counted.

blocks.html: After Shays' Rebellion, twelve states sent delegates to Philadelphia (Rhode Island stayed away). From May 25 to September 17, 1787, 55 delegates met in the same building where the Declaration had been signed, with George Washington presiding. They were sent to revise the Articles. Instead they wrote a new constitution.

The Virginia Plan (James Madison's ideas) wanted a strong government with seats in Congress by population. The New Jersey Plan wanted equal votes for every state. The Great (Connecticut) Compromise did both: the House by population, the Senate with two members per state. Other compromises dealt with slavery, trade and the presidency.

Big states and small states each had a fair point. Virginia said a vote should count the same for every citizen, so more people should mean more seats. Delaware said the states were equals that had joined by choice, and a small state would be swallowed. Two houses let both principles stand. The vote on July 16, 1787, passed by a single state.

cards.text: Seats in both houses by population
One house, one vote per state
Kept the Articles but added powers to tax and regulate trade
A single President chosen by electors

blocks.html: Nearly one in five people in the states was enslaved, most in the South. Southern delegates wanted enslaved people counted for seats in the House; Northern delegates did not want them counted for seats if they were not counted as people with rights. The Three-Fifths Compromise counted "three fifths of all other Persons" (enslaved people) for House seats and direct taxes. The Convention also barred Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808 and required that people who escaped slavery be returned. The word "slavery" does not appear in the Constitution of 1787.

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Article I, Section 2, Clause 3 held the three-fifths rule. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) replaced it.

blocks.title: Working the three-fifths rule
blocks.q: A state has 300,000 free people and 100,000 enslaved people. What population counts for its House seats under the three-fifths rule?
steps: Count three of every five enslaved people: 100,000 × 3/5 = 60,000.

blocks.html: A common error is to say the Constitution declared enslaved people "three-fifths of a person" in law. The clause was a counting rule for House seats and direct taxes. It gave the slaveholding states more seats, while enslaved people themselves had no vote and no rights under it. Check: whose power grew because of the count? The slaveholders'.

The delegates also invented a single President chosen by electors, gave Congress the power to tax and regulate trade, and set up a Supreme Court. On September 17, 39 delegates signed. Then the fight over ratification began.
